workEn: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi
title: Pwyll Pendeuic Dyuet
titleEn: Pwyll, Prince of Dyfed — Gwawl and the bag
source: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, First Branch, from the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth 4, c. 1350) as printed in J. Gwenogvryn Evans, The White Book Mabinogion (Pwllheli, 1907), columns 19–27; public domain. Readings are the manuscript's as Evans prints them, checked against the page images; word division, punctuation, capitals and quotation marks are ours. Where the White Book omits a word the sense requires, it is supplied from the Red Book (Rhŷs & Evans) and the note says so. Pronunciation convention: the manuscript spelling read with the sounds of Welsh c. 1300. Translations made fresh from the Welsh.

sentences.t: A guahanu a wnaethont, a chyrchu a wnaeth ef parth a'e teulu a'e niuer.
sentences.l: And parting they-did, and making-for he-did towards his household-troop and his company.
sentences.i: And they parted, and he made his way back to his warband and his company.
sentences.n: The part opens where the last ended: Pwyll and Rhiannon part. guahanu a wnaethont 'parting they did' is the verbal-noun narrative: a verbal noun, then a with a form of gwneuthur 'do' — wnaethont is its third-person plural preterite, soft-mutated after a. a chyrchu 'and making for' shows the spirant mutation after a 'and' (kyrchu). parth a 'towards'; a'e is a + 'e 'his'. teulu is the lord's household-troop, his armed following; niuer 'company, host'. Old spelling: gu = gw (guahanu = gwahanu). teulu after 'e 'his' would be softened (a'e deulu); the mutation is not written here, and the Red Book has the same.

sentences.t: Pa ymouyn bynnac a uei ganthunt wy y wrth y uorwyn, y chwedleu ereill y trossei ynteu.
sentences.l: Whatever inquiry that would-be with-them, them, about the maiden, to other tales he-for-his-part would-turn.
sentences.i: Whatever questions his men had about the maiden, he would turn them aside to other talk.
sentences.n: Pa … bynnac 'whatever'. a uei 'that might be' is bei, the imperfect subjunctive of bot 'be', soft-mutated after the relative a (b > u). ganthunt wy 'with them' is the conjugated preposition gan 'with', third person plural, with the pronoun wy repeated after it. y wrth 'from, about'. y uorwyn 'the maiden': morwyn, soft-mutated after the article because it is feminine singular. The sentence puts an adverbial phrase first (y chwedleu ereill 'to other tales'), so the verb takes the particle y. trossei is the third-person imperfect of trossi (modern trosi) 'turn', a verb beside troi (the Red Book also has y trossei): 'he would turn (it)', of a habit. ynteu 'he for his part'. Spelling: u = v (uei, uorwyn).

sentences.t: Odyna treulaw y ulwydyn hyt yr amser a wnaethont; ac ymgueiraw ar y ganuet marchauc.
sentences.l: Thereafter spending the year until the time they-did; and equipping-himself on his hundredth horseman.
sentences.i: Then they spent the year until the appointed time; and he made himself ready, one of a hundred horsemen.
sentences.n: Odyna 'from there, thereafter'. treulaw … a wnaethont 'spending … they did' = they spent; y ulwydyn 'the year' is blwydyn, feminine, soft-mutated after the article. ymgueiraw (ymgyweiraw) 'make oneself ready, equip oneself' has the reflexive prefix ym-. ar y ganuet marchauc 'on his hundredth horseman' is an idiom: he himself made up the hundred — he rode with ninety-nine others. canuet 'hundredth' is soft-mutated after y 'his' (k > g). marchauc = marchawc 'horseman'.

sentences.t: Ef a aeth ryngtaw a llys Eueyd Hen, ac ef a doeth y'r llys, a llawen uuwyt wrthaw, a dygyuor a llewenyd ac arlwy mawr a oed yn y erbyn, a holl uaranned y llys wrth y gynghor ef y treulwyt.
sentences.l: He it-was-that went between-himself and the court of Hefeydd the-Old, and he it-was-that came to the court, and glad was-it-been towards-him, and a gathering and rejoicing and a great banquet that-was against-him, and all the wealth of the court at his counsel was-spent.
sentences.i: He made his way to the court of Hefeydd the Old and came to the court, and he was gladly received; a gathering and rejoicing and a great banquet were waiting for him, and all the wealth of the court was spent as he directed.
sentences.n: Ef a aeth 'he went' is the abnormal sentence, the tale's ordinary narrative order: subject first, then the particle a, then the verb. It stresses nothing. aeth ryngtaw a 'went between himself and' is the idiom for setting off to a place; ryngtaw is the conjugated preposition y rwng 'between', third person masculine. Eueyd Hen is Hefeydd the Old, Rhiannon's father (spelt Heueyd below). llawen uuwyt wrthaw 'glad it-was-been towards him': uuwyt is buwyt, the impersonal preterite of bot (-wyt), soft-mutated after the fronted adjective — 'he was welcomed'. yn y erbyn 'against him' = ready for his coming. holl uaranned 'all the wealth' (maranned, soft after holl). y treulwyt 'was spent' is another impersonal preterite in -wyt.

sentences.t: Kyweiryaw y neuad a wnaethpwyt, ac y'r bordeu yd aethant.
sentences.l: Preparing the hall was-done, and to the tables they-went.
sentences.i: The hall was made ready, and they went to the tables.
sentences.n: Kyweiryaw … a wnaethpwyt: the verbal-noun pattern again, but with wnaethpwyt, the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur — 'preparing was done'. Spelling: k = c (kyweiryaw = cyweirio). y'r bordeu 'to the tables'. Because the sentence opens with that phrase, the verb takes the particle yd (the form of y before a vowel): yd aethant 'they went'.

sentences.t: Sef ual yd eistedyssont, Heueyd Hen ar neill law Pwyll, a Riannon o'r parth arall idaw; y am hynny pawb ual y bei y enryded.
sentences.l: That-is how they-sat: Hefeydd the-Old on one hand of Pwyll, and Rhiannon from the other side to-him; around that, everyone as his rank might-be.
sentences.i: They sat with Hefeydd the Old on one side of Pwyll and Rhiannon on his other side; and beyond them everyone according to his rank.
sentences.n: Sef 'that is' introduces the answer to an implied question — how did they sit? eistedyssont 'they sat' is a third-person plural preterite in -yssont. Spelling: d = dd (eisted-, Heueyd), u = v (Heueyd = Hefeydd). ar neill law 'on one hand'; o'r parth arall idaw 'on the other side of him' — idaw is y 'to' conjugated, third person masculine. Riannon is the manuscript's spelling of Rhiannon. y am hynny 'around that, beyond that'. ual y bei y enryded 'as his rank might be': bei is the imperfect subjunctive of bot, and enryded is anryded 'rank' spelt with e.

sentences.t: Bwyta a chyuedach ac ymdidan a wnaethont.
sentences.l: Eating and carousing and conversing they-did.
sentences.i: They ate and drank and talked.
sentences.n: Three verbal nouns closed by a wnaethont 'they did'. a chyuedach shows the spirant mutation after a 'and' (kyuedach 'drinking together, carousal'). ymdidan 'conversing' has the prefix ym- of mutual action.

sentences.t: Ac ar dechreu kyuedach gwedy bwyt, wynt a welynt yn dyuot y mywn, guas gwineu, mawr, teyrneid, a guisc o bali amdanaw.
sentences.l: And at the beginning of carousing after food, they it-was-that saw coming in a youth auburn, big, princely, and a garment of brocade about-him.
sentences.i: And at the start of the drinking after the meal, they saw coming in a tall, auburn-haired, princely young man, wearing a garment of brocade.
sentences.n: wynt a welynt 'they saw' — subject, a, verb again; welynt is the imperfect plural of gwelet, soft-mutated after a. yn dyuot y mywn 'coming in'. guas 'young man' (gwas) is followed by three adjectives: gwineu 'auburn, chestnut-brown', mawr 'big', teyrneid 'princely' (teyrn 'ruler'). o bali 'of brocade': pali 'silk brocade', soft-mutated after o. amdanaw 'about him' is am conjugated, third person masculine — clothing is 'about' you. Spelling: -t = -d (bwyt = bwyd).

sentences.t: A phan doeth y gynted y neuad, kyuarch guell a oruc y Pwyll a'y gedymdeithon.
sentences.l: And when he-came to the upper-end of the hall, greeting he-did to Pwyll and his companions.
sentences.i: And when he came to the upper end of the hall, he greeted Pwyll and his companions.
sentences.n: A phan 'and when': pan with the spirant mutation after a. y gynted 'to the upper end': kynted, soft-mutated after y 'to', is the top of the hall, where the lord and his chief guests sat. kyuarch guell 'greet', literally 'ask better', to wish someone well; a oruc is the preterite of gwneuthur, 'he did'. y Pwyll 'to Pwyll': y 'to' should soften a following word, but proper names are often left unmutated in the writing. a'y gedymdeithon 'and his companions' (kedymdeithon, soft after 'y 'his').

sentences.t: “Cressaw Duw wrthyt, eneit, a dos y eisted,” heb y Pwyll.
sentences.l: “Welcome of-God to-you, soul, and go to sit,” said Pwyll.
sentences.i: “God's welcome to you, friend, and go and sit down,” said Pwyll.
sentences.n: Cressaw (modern croeso) 'welcome'; Cressaw Duw wrthyt 'God's welcome to you' is a fixed greeting, and wrthyt is wrth 'towards' conjugated, second person singular. eneit 'soul' is a friendly form of address. dos is the imperative of mynet 'go'; y eisted 'to sit'. heb y Pwyll: after heb 'said' a name often takes the article y, as throughout the tale.

sentences.t: “Nac af,” heb ef, “eirchat wyf, a'm neges a wnaf.”
sentences.l: “I-will-not-go,” said he; “a-petitioner am-I, and my errand I-will-do.”
sentences.i: “I will not,” he said. “I come as a petitioner, and I will do my errand.”
sentences.n: Nac af 'I will not go': Welsh answers by repeating the verb, and nac (na before a vowel) is the negative of answers and commands. eirchat wyf 'a petitioner I am' — the predicate comes first, before the verb 'to be'; eirchat is one who asks (erchi 'ask'). a'm neges a wnaf 'and my errand I will do': a 'and' + 'm 'my', then the object put first and the relative a before the verb.

sentences.t: “Gwna yn llawen,” heb y Pwyll.
sentences.l: “Do gladly,” said Pwyll.
sentences.i: “Do so, and gladly,” said Pwyll.
sentences.n: Gwna is the imperative of gwneuthur 'do'. yn llawen 'gladly' is the adjective llawen 'glad' made an adverb with yn; it recurs through the part as the courteous word of assent.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ef, “wrthyt ti y mae uy neges i, ac y erchi it y dodwyf.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he, “towards you is my errand, and to ask of-you I-have-come.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “my errand is to you, and I have come to make a request of you.”
sentences.n: wrthyt ti y mae 'to you it is' — the phrase is put first, so the verb mae takes the particle y. uy neges i 'my errand' with the reinforcing pronoun i after the noun. y erchi it 'to ask (of) you': it is y 'to' conjugated, second person singular. dodwyf 'I have come' is an old first-person perfect of dyuot 'come', beside the preterite deuthum (the Red Book has dodwyf too); it is used again below.

sentences.t: “Pa arch bynnac a erchych di ymi, hyt y gallwyf y gaffael, itti y byd.”
sentences.l: “Whatever request you-may-ask to-me, as-far-as I-may-be-able to-get-it, to-you it-will-be.”
sentences.i: “Whatever request you make of me, so far as I am able to get it, it shall be yours.”
sentences.n: Pwyll speaks, though the tale gives no tag. Pa arch bynnac 'whatever request'. a erchych di 'that you may ask' — erchych is the present subjunctive of erchi, since the request is not yet made. hyt y gallwyf 'as far as I may be able' (gallwyf, present subjunctive of gallu). y gaffael 'its getting' = to get it: the object of a verbal noun is a possessive before it, and y 'its' softens kaffael. itti y byd 'to you it will be' — byd is the future of bot.

sentences.t: “Och!” heb y Riannon, “paham y rody di attep y uelly?”
sentences.l: “Och!” said Rhiannon, “why do-you-give answer thus?”
sentences.i: “Oh!” said Rhiannon, “why do you answer like that?”
sentences.n: Och is a cry of dismay. paham 'why' (pa ham 'for what'). y rody di 'you give': rody is the second-person present of rodi 'give'. y uelly 'thus' (modern felly), written here with the particle y before it.

sentences.t: “Neus rodes y uelly, Arglwydes, yg gwyd gwyrda,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “He-has-given-it thus, Lady, in the presence of noblemen,” said he.
sentences.i: “He has given it so, Lady, in the presence of noblemen,” he said.
sentences.n: The suitor answers for Pwyll. Neus is the affirmative particle neu with the infixed pronoun 's 'it': neus rodes 'he has given it'; rodes is the third-person preterite of rodi. Arglwydes 'Lady'. yg gwyd 'in the presence of': yn 'in' + gwyd 'presence', the n of yn becoming ng before g (modern yng ngŵydd). gwyrda 'noblemen' (gwyr + da 'good men').

sentences.t: “Eneit,” heb y Pwyll, “beth yw dy arch di?”
sentences.l: “Soul,” said Pwyll, “what is your request?”
sentences.i: “Friend,” said Pwyll, “what is your request?”
sentences.n: beth 'what' is peth 'thing' soft-mutated, the usual form in questions. dy arch di 'your request', with di repeating 'your' after the noun. arch 'request, petition' is the noun of erchi.

sentences.t: “Y wreic uwyaf a garaf yd wyt yn kyscu heno genthi. Ac y herchi hi a'r arlwy a'r darmerth yssyd ymma y dodwyf i.”
sentences.l: “The woman most that I-love, you-are sleeping tonight with-her. And to ask-for her, and the banquet and the preparation that-is here, I-have-come.”
sentences.i: “The woman I love most — you are to sleep with her tonight. And it is to ask for her, and for the banquet and the preparations that are here, that I have come.”
sentences.n: Y wreic uwyaf a garaf 'the woman most that I love': gwreic soft after the feminine article, mwyaf 'most' soft after the feminine noun, karaf 'I love' soft after the relative a. The phrase is put first and then picked up by genthi 'with her' (gan conjugated, third person feminine). y herchi hi 'to ask for her': y 'her' puts h before a vowel (erchi). arlwy 'banquet, provision'; darmerth 'preparation'. yssyd 'which is' is the relative form of bot.

sentences.t: Kynhewi a oruc Pwyll, cany bu attep a rodassei.
sentences.l: Falling-silent Pwyll did, since there-was-not an-answer that he-had-given.
sentences.i: Pwyll fell silent, for there was no answer he could give.
sentences.n: Kynhewi a oruc 'he fell silent' — verbal noun + a oruc. cany 'since … not' (can 'since' + ny 'not'). rodassei is a pluperfect (-assei), a tense modern Welsh has lost; here it has a modal sense, 'that he could have given'.

sentences.t: “Taw, hyt y mynnych,” heb y Riannon, “ny bu uuscrellach gwr ar y ssynnwyr e hun nog ry uuost ti.”
sentences.l: “Be-silent as-long-as you-wish,” said Rhiannon, “there-was-not a more-feeble man on his wits himself than you-have-been.”
sentences.i: “Be silent as long as you like,” said Rhiannon. “There was never a man more feeble with his own wits than you have been.”
sentences.n: Taw is the imperative of tewi 'be silent'; hyt y mynnych 'as long as you may wish' (mynnych, present subjunctive of mynnu). uuscrellach 'more feeble, more inept', comparative of muscrell, soft-mutated as the predicate after ny bu. ar y ssynnwyr e hun 'on his own sense' — ss is just a spelling of s (synnwyr 'sense'). nog 'than'. ry uuost 'you have been': ry is the perfective particle and softens buost, second-person preterite of bot.

sentences.t: “Arglwydes,” heb ef, “ny wydwn i pwy oed ef.”
sentences.l: “Lady,” said he, “I-did-not-know who he was.”
sentences.i: “Lady,” he said, “I did not know who he was.”
sentences.n: ny wydwn 'I did not know': wydwn is the first-person imperfect of gwybot, soft-mutated after ny 'not'. pwy oed ef 'who he was' — oed is the imperfect of bot.

sentences.t: “Llyna y gwr y mynyssit uy rodi i idaw o'm hanuod,” heb hi, “Guawl uab Clut, gwr tormynnawc, kyuoethawc. A chan derw yt dywedut y geir a dywedeist, dyro ui idaw rac anglot yt.”
sentences.l: “There-is the man that it-had-been-wished to-give me to-him against-my will,” said she, “Gwawl son of-Clud, a man of-great-following(?), wealthy. And since it-has-happened to-you to-say the word you-said, give me to-him for-fear-of dishonour to-you.”
sentences.i: “That is the man they meant to give me to against my will,” she said: “Gwawl son of Clud, a man of great following and great wealth. And since it has befallen you to say the word you said, give me to him, lest dishonour fall on you.”
sentences.n: Llyna 'there is, that is' (beside llyma 'here is'). y mynyssit 'that it had been wished': mynyssit is the impersonal pluperfect of mynnu (-ssit), 'they had wanted'. uy rodi i 'my giving' = to give me. o'm hanuod 'against my will': o + 'm 'my', which puts h before a vowel; anuod is an- 'un-' + bod 'will'. Guawl uab Clut is Gwawl son of Clud, mab softened after the name. tormynnawc is a rare word of disputed meaning: it is usually taken as 'with a great host' (torf 'crowd'), 'mighty', but that is not certain. chan derw yt 'since it has befallen you' — can 'since' with spirant mutation after a; derw is deryw, the old third-person perfect of daruot 'happen', 'it has happened' (the Red Book also writes derw). dyro is the imperative of rodi; ui is mi 'me' softened. rac anglot 'for fear of dishonour' (an- + clot 'fame').

sentences.t: “Arglwydes,” heb ef, “ny wnn i pa ryw attep yw hwnnw. Ny allaf ui arnaf a dywedy di uyth.”
sentences.l: “Lady,” said he, “I-do-not-know what kind of answer is that. I-cannot, I, on-me what you-say ever.”
sentences.i: “Lady,” he said, “I do not know what kind of answer that is. I could never bring myself to do what you say.”
sentences.n: ny wnn 'I do not know' — gwnn, softened after ny. pa ryw 'what kind'. hwnnw 'that' (masculine). Ny allaf ui arnaf 'I cannot, I, upon myself' is an idiom: 'I cannot bring myself (to do)'; allaf is gallaf softened after ny, ui is the pronoun mi softened, and arnaf is ar conjugated, first person. a dywedy di 'what you say' (dywedy, second-person present).

sentences.t: “Dyro di ui idaw ef,” heb hi, “a mi a wnaf na chaffo ef uiui uyth.”
sentences.l: “Give you me to-him,” said she, “and I it-is-that will-make that he-shall-not-have me ever.”
sentences.i: “Give me to him,” she said, “and I will see to it that he never has me.”
sentences.n: Dyro di ui 'give, you, me' — the imperative with its subject di and its object ui (mi softened). mi a wnaf 'I will make (it)'. na chaffo 'that he may not get': kaffo is the present subjunctive of caffael, with the spirant mutation after na. uiui is the doubled emphatic pronoun miui 'me myself', softened.

sentences.t: “Pa furyf uyd hynny?” heb y Pwyll.
sentences.l: “What form will-be that?” said Pwyll.
sentences.i: “How will that be?” said Pwyll.
sentences.n: Pa furyf 'what form?' = how? (ffuryf 'form', the scribe writing f for ff as before). uyd is byd 'will be', soft-mutated after the question word.

sentences.t: “Mi a rodaf i'th law got uechan,” heb hi, “a chadw honno gennyt yn da. Ac ef a eirch y wled a'r arlwy a'r darmerth. Ac nit oes y'th uedyant di hynny.
sentences.l: “I it-is-that will-give into-your hand a small bag,” said she, “and keep that with-you well. And he it-is-that will-ask the feast and the banquet and the preparation. And there-is-not in your power that.
sentences.i: “I will put a little bag into your hand,” she said, “and keep it safe by you. He will ask for the feast and the banquet and the preparations. And that is not in your power to give.
sentences.n: Rhiannon's long speech of instruction runs across the next units. i'th law 'into your hand' (i = y 'to, into' + 'th 'your'). got uechan 'a small bag': cot 'bag' is softened as the object of the verb, and bechan, the feminine of bychan 'small', is softened after the feminine noun; honno 'that' is the feminine to match. a chadw 'and keep' (kadw, spirant after a), an imperative. a eirch 'will ask': eirch is the third-person present of erchi. y wled 'the feast' (gwled, feminine). y'th uedyant 'in your power': medyant softened after 'th 'your'. nit oes 'there is not'.

sentences.t: A mi ui a rodaf y wled y'r teulu a'r niueroed,” heb hi, “a hwnnw uyd dy attep am hynny.
sentences.l: And I myself it-is-that will-give the feast to the household-troop and the companies,” said she, “and that will-be your answer about that.
sentences.i: And I myself will give the feast to the warband and the companies,” she said, “and that will be your answer to that.
sentences.n: mi ui 'I, myself' — the pronoun doubled for emphasis, the second softened. a rodaf 'will give', present tense with future sense. y'r teulu 'to the household-troop'; niueroed is the plural of niuer 'company, host'. hwnnw uyd 'that will be' — byd softened as after the relative a, which is often left unwritten before forms of bot.

sentences.t: Amdanaf innheu,” heb hi, “mi a wnaf oet ac ef, ulwydyn y heno, y gyscu gennyf; ac ym penn y ulwydyn,” heb hi, “byd ditheu a'r got honn genhyt, ar dy ganuet marchawc yn y perllan uchot.
sentences.l: About-me for-my-part,” said she, “I it-is-that will-make a-tryst with him, a-year from tonight, to sleep with-me; and at the end of the year,” said she, “be you-for-your-part and this bag with-you, on your hundredth horseman in the orchard above.
sentences.i: As for me,” she said, “I will make a tryst with him a year from tonight, to sleep with me; and at the end of the year,” she said, “be there yourself with this bag, one of a hundred horsemen, in the orchard up yonder.
sentences.n: Amdanaf innheu 'about me, for my part': am conjugated, first person, with the conjunctive pronoun innheu. oet 'tryst, appointed time'. ulwydyn y heno 'a year from tonight': blwydyn softened as an expression of time. ym penn y ulwydyn 'at the head of the year' = at the year's end; ym is yn 'in' before p. byd ditheu 'be you (for your part)': byd here is the second-person imperative of bot, and titheu softens after it. genhyt is another spelling of gennyt 'with you'. ar dy ganuet marchawc 'on your hundredth horseman' = one of a hundred (kanuet softened after dy). yn y perllan: perllan 'orchard' is feminine and would normally soften after the article (y berllan, as written later); here it stands unmutated. uchot 'above, up yonder'.

sentences.t: A phan uo ef ar perued y digrifwch a'y gyuedach dyret titheu dy hun y mywn a dillat reudus amdanat, a'r got y'th law,” heb hi, “ac nac arch dim namyn lloneit y got o uwyt.
sentences.l: And when he-may-be at the middle of the amusement and his carousing, come you-for-your-part yourself in with clothes ragged(?) about-you, and the bag in-your hand,” said she, “and do-not-ask anything but the-fill of the bag of food.
sentences.i: And when he is in the midst of his pleasure and his drinking, come in yourself, in ragged clothes, with the bag in your hand,” she said, “and ask for nothing but the bag's fill of food.
sentences.n: pan uo 'when he may be': bo, present subjunctive of bot, softened after pan. ar perued 'at the middle' — ar normally softens (ar berued); the writing leaves it unmutated. digrifwch 'amusement, pleasure'. dyret is the imperative of dyuot 'come'; dy hun 'yourself'. reudus is a rare word: it is generally taken to mean 'ragged, shabby' from the context of a beggar's disguise, but its meaning is not certainly known. nac arch 'do not ask' is the negative imperative of erchi. namyn 'but, except'. lloneit 'fill, fullness' (llawn 'full'); o uwyt 'of food' (bwyt softened after o).

sentences.t: Minheu,” heb hi, “a baraf, bei dottit yssyd yn y seith cantref hynn o uwyt a llynn yndi, na bydei launach no chynt.
sentences.l: I-for-my-part,” said she, “it-is-that will-cause, were-there-put what-is in these seven cantrefs of food and drink in-it, that it-would-not-be fuller than before.
sentences.i: And I,” she said, “will see to it that, were all the food and drink in these seven cantrefs put into it, it would be no fuller than before.
sentences.n: Minheu … a baraf 'I for my part will cause': peri 'cause', softened after a. bei dottit 'if there were put': bei here is 'if' (pei), and dottit is the impersonal imperfect subjunctive of dodi 'put': the ending is -hit, and d + h gives tt (the Red Book reads pei dottit). yssyd 'what is'. y seith cantref hynn 'these seven cantrefs': hynn 'these' points to the land where they stand, Hefeydd's; Dyfed too is reckoned seven cantrefs, but that is not what is said here. llynn 'drink'. yndi 'in it' is yn conjugated, third person feminine, for the feminine cot. na bydei launach 'that it would not be fuller': bydei is the habitual imperfect of bot (modern byddai), 'would be', in the result of an unreal condition (the Red Book has na bo), and llawnach, comparative of llawn, softens as the predicate. no chynt 'than before', spirant after no.

sentences.t: A guedy byryer llawer yndi, ef a ouyn yt, ‘A uyd llawn dy got ti uyth?’
sentences.l: And after there-be-thrown much into-it, he it-is-that will-ask to-you, ‘Will-be full your bag ever?’
sentences.i: And when a great deal has been thrown in, he will ask you, ‘Will your bag ever be full?’
sentences.n: guedy byryer 'after there be thrown': byryer is the impersonal present subjunctive of bwrw 'throw' (-er). a ouyn 'will ask': gouyn, third-person present, loses its g under soft mutation after a. yt 'to you'. A uyd 'will … be?': a is the question particle and softens byd. Speech within speech is in single quotes.

sentences.t: Dywet titheu, ‘Na uyd, ony chyuyt dylyedauc tra chyuoethauc, a guascu a'y deudroet y bwyt yn y got, a dywedut, “Digawn ry dodet ymman.”’
sentences.l: Say you-for-your-part, ‘It-will-not-be, unless there-rises a nobleman exceedingly wealthy, and pressing with his two-feet the food in the bag, and saying, “Enough has-been-put here.”’
sentences.i: Say to him, ‘No, not unless a nobleman of great wealth rises and presses the food down in the bag with both his feet, and says, “Enough has been put in here.”’
sentences.n: Dywet is the imperative of dywedut 'say'. Na uyd 'it will not be' — 'no' by repeating the verb. ony chyuyt 'unless rises': kyuyt is the third-person present of kyuodi 'rise', with the spirant mutation after ony 'unless'. dylyedauc 'a man of rank, a nobleman by birth' (dylyet 'right, entitlement'). tra chyuoethauc 'exceedingly wealthy': tra 'very' gives the spirant mutation. guascu 'press'; a'y deudroet 'with his two feet' (deu 'two' + troet, softened). Digawn ry dodet 'enough has been put': dodet is the impersonal preterite of dodi (-et), made perfect by ry. ymman = yma 'here'. A third level of speech goes in double quotes.

sentences.t: A minheu a baraf idaw ef uynet y sseghi y bwyt yn y got.
sentences.l: And I-for-my-part it-is-that will-cause to-him going to tread the food in the bag.
sentences.i: And I will make him go and tread the food down in the bag.
sentences.n: a baraf idaw ef uynet 'I will cause to him to go' = I will make him go: mynet softened as the object of paraf. sseghi is sengi 'tread' — ss for s, and g for the sound ng, as the scribe often writes it.

sentences.t: A phan el ef, tro ditheu y got, yny el ef dros y pen yn y got.
sentences.l: And when he-may-go, turn you-for-your-part the bag, until he-may-go over his head into the bag.
sentences.i: And when he does, turn the bag up until he goes over his head into it.
sentences.n: pan el 'when he may go': el is the present subjunctive of mynet. tro is the imperative of troi 'turn'; ditheu is titheu softened after the verb. yny el 'until he may go' — yny 'until' takes the subjunctive of a future event. dros y pen 'over his head': tros softened; pen is penn spelt with one n.

sentences.t: Ac yna llad glwm ar garryeu y got.
sentences.l: And then tie a-knot on the thongs of the bag.
sentences.i: And then tie a knot in the thongs of the bag.
sentences.n: llad here is the imperative, the same form as the verbal noun llad 'strike, cut, kill'; llad clwm 'strike a knot' is the idiom for tying one. glwm is clwm softened as the object; garryeu is carryeu 'thongs, laces' softened after ar.

sentences.t: A bit corn canu da am dy uynwgyl, a phan uo ef yn rwymedic yn y got, dot titheu lef ar dy gorn, a bit hynny yn arwyd y rot a'th uarchogyon; pan glywhont llef dy gorn, diskynnent wynteu am pen y llys.”
sentences.l: And let-there-be a horn of-sounding good about your neck, and when he-may-be bound in the bag, put you-for-your-part a-cry on your horn, and let-be that as a-sign between-you and your horsemen; when they-may-hear the cry of your horn, let-them-descend they-for-their-part upon the court.”
sentences.i: And have a good horn for sounding about your neck, and when he is bound in the bag, sound a blast on your horn, and let that be the sign between you and your horsemen: when they hear the blast of your horn, let them come down upon the court.”
sentences.n: bit is the third-person imperative of bot, 'let there be'. corn canu 'a horn of sounding'. uynwgyl is mynwgyl 'neck', softened after dy. yn rwymedic 'bound', with the predicative yn (rh- is not softened after yn). dot is the imperative of dodi; dot lef ar dy gorn 'put a cry on your horn' = sound it (llef softened as the object, corn after dy). y rot a 'between you and' is y rwng conjugated, second person, as in y rof i a Duw 'between me and God'. glywhont 'they may hear', present subjunctive plural of klywet. diskynnent 'let them descend' is a third-person plural imperative (-ent). am pen y llys: Evans prints pen with p, as the manuscript has it — this is penn 'head, top', and am penn 'down upon'; the soft mutation one would expect after am (am ben) is not written here; the Red Book has am benn.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb y Guawl, “madws oed ymi cael attep am a ercheis.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said Gwawl, “it-is-time it-was for-me getting an-answer about what I-asked.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” said Gwawl, “it is time I had an answer to what I asked.”
sentences.n: The scene shifts back to Gwawl. madws is a word of uncertain origin and exact force; it is generally taken to mean 'it is time, it is fitting', and the sense here needs no more. oed 'was' with a conditional colour. cael is caffael 'get', in the shortened form. am a ercheis 'about what I asked': ercheis is the first-person preterite of erchi.

sentences.t: “Kymeint ac a ercheist,” heb y Pwyll, “o'r a uo y'm medyant i, ti a'y keffy.”
sentences.l: “As-much as you-asked,” said Pwyll, “of what may-be in my power, you it-is-that will-get-it.”
sentences.i: “All that you asked,” said Pwyll, “so far as it is in my power, you shall have.”
sentences.n: Kymeint ac a ercheist 'as much as you asked' (ercheist, second-person preterite). o'r a uo 'of what may be' — the article with the relative a, 'that which', and bo softened. y'm medyant 'in my power'. ti a'y keffy 'you will get it': 'y is the infixed object 'it', and keffy the second-person present of caffael.

sentences.t: “Eneit,” heb hitheu Riannon, “am y wled a'r darpar yssyd yma, hwnnw a rodeis i y wyr Dyuet ac y'r teulu, a'r yniueroed yssyd ymma. Hwnnw nit eidawaf y rodi y neb.
sentences.l: “Soul,” said she-for-her-part Rhiannon, “about the feast and the provision that-is here, that I-gave to the men of-Dyfed and to the household-troop, and the companies that-are here. That I-do-not-own to give to anyone.
sentences.i: “Friend,” said Rhiannon, “as for the feast and the provision that are here, I have given that to the men of Dyfed and to the warband, and to the companies that are here. That is not mine to give to anyone.
sentences.n: Rhiannon answers for Pwyll, addressing Gwawl. heb hitheu Riannon 'said she for her part, Rhiannon' — the conjunctive pronoun and the name together. darpar 'provision'. hwnnw a rodeis i 'that I gave': object first, then a and the verb; rodeis is the first-person preterite of rodi. y wyr Dyuet 'to the men of Dyfed' — gwyr softened after y 'to'. yniueroed is niueroed with a prefixed y. nit eidawaf is uncertain: it appears to be a first-person verb made from eidaw 'his own, property', 'I do not own (it)', 'it is not mine', a form not otherwise known. The Red Book reads instead nyt adawaf i y rodi y neb, with adawaf from adaw 'leave, allow', 'I will not allow it to be given to anyone'. The l and i follow the White Book reading as glossed here, which is a guess.

sentences.t: Blwydyn y heno ynteu, y byd gwled darparedic yn y llys honn i titheu, eneit, y gyscu gennyf innheu.”
sentences.l: A-year from tonight however, there-will-be a feast prepared in this court for you-for-your-part, soul, to sleep with-me for-my-part.”
sentences.i: A year from tonight, though, there will be a feast made ready for you in this court, friend, and you shall sleep with me.”
sentences.n: Blwydyn y heno 'a year from tonight', as above. ynteu here is an adverb, 'then, however'. darparedic 'prepared', a participle in -edic. y llys honn 'this court': llys is treated as feminine (honn). i titheu 'for you'; y gyscu 'to sleep' (kyscu softened after y). gennyf innheu 'with me' — gan conjugated, first person, and the conjunctive pronoun.

sentences.t: Gwawl a gerdawd ryngthaw a'y gyuoeth.
sentences.l: Gwawl it-was-that went between-himself and his realm.
sentences.i: Gwawl went off to his realm.
sentences.n: a gerdawd 'went' (kerdet 'walk, go'): -awd is an old third-person preterite ending, beside -wys. ryngthaw a'y gyuoeth 'between himself and his realm' is the same idiom of setting off as aeth ryngtaw a above; kyuoeth 'realm' softened after 'y 'his'.

sentences.t: Pwyll ynteu a doeth y Dyuet.
sentences.l: Pwyll for-his-part it-was-that came to Dyfed.
sentences.i: Pwyll, for his part, came to Dyfed.
sentences.n: ynteu after the name marks the switch of subject: 'Pwyll for his part'. y Dyuet 'to Dyfed' (Dyuet: u = v, -t = -d); y 'to' softens, but d to dd does not show in this spelling.

sentences.t: A'r ulwydyn honno a dreulwys pawb o honunt hyt oet y wled a oed yn llys Eueyd Hen.
sentences.l: And that year it-was-that spent each of-them until the time of the feast that was in the court of Hefeydd the-Old.
sentences.i: And they all spent that year until the time of the feast at the court of Hefeydd the Old.
sentences.n: Here the object comes first: A'r ulwydyn honno a dreulwys 'and that year … spent' — the abnormal sentence with the object fronted; the subject, pawb o honunt 'each of them', follows the verb. dreulwys is treulwys softened after a; -wys is the old third-person preterite. o honunt 'of them' is o conjugated, third person plural. oet y wled 'the appointed time of the feast'.

sentences.t: Gwaul uab Clut a doeth parth a'r wled a oed darparedic idaw, a chyrchu y llys a wnaeth, a llawen uuwyt wrthaw.
sentences.l: Gwawl son of-Clud it-was-that came towards the feast that was prepared for-him, and making-for the court he-did, and glad was-it-been towards-him.
sentences.i: Gwawl son of Clud came to the feast that had been prepared for him, made for the court, and was gladly received.
sentences.n: Gwaul is another spelling of Gwawl. a doeth 'came', preterite of dyuot. a chyrchu … a wnaeth 'and making for … he did'. llawen uuwyt wrthaw 'he was gladly received' — the impersonal formula used of Pwyll's arrival a year before.

sentences.t: Pwyll ynteu Penn Annwn a doeth y'r berllan ar y ganuet marchauc, ual y gorchymynnassei Riannon idaw, a'r got ganthaw.
sentences.l: Pwyll for-his-part Head of-Annwfn it-was-that came to the orchard on his hundredth horseman, as Rhiannon had-commanded to-him, and the bag with-him.
sentences.i: Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, came to the orchard, one of a hundred horsemen, as Rhiannon had bidden him, with the bag.
sentences.n: Penn Annwn is the title Pwyll won in the first part, 'Head of Annwfn'; the manuscript spells the name Annwn here, not Annwuyn as in the first part (the Red Book has Annwuyn here); it is the same name, Annwfn. y'r berllan 'to the orchard': perllan, feminine, softened after the article as expected this time. ar y ganuet marchauc, the 'hundredth horseman' idiom again. gorchymynnassei 'had commanded' is the pluperfect in -assei. ganthaw 'with him' is gan conjugated, third person masculine.

sentences.t: Gwiscaw bratteu trwm ymdanw a oruc Pwyll, a chymryt lloppaneu mawr am y draet.
sentences.l: Putting-on rags heavy about-him did Pwyll, and taking big clumsy-boots on his feet.
sentences.i: Pwyll put heavy rags on himself and big clumsy boots on his feet.
sentences.n: Gwiscaw … a oruc 'putting on … he did'. bratteu 'rags'; trwm 'heavy' stays unmutated after a plural noun. ymdanw is as the manuscript writes it, without an a: a slip or contraction for ymdanaw 'about him', am conjugated, third person masculine (the Red Book has ymdanaw). lloppaneu are rough, shapeless boots or foot-wrappings — a beggar's footwear. y draet 'his feet' (traet softened after y 'his').

sentences.t: A phan wybu y bot ar dechreu kyuedach wedy bwyta, dyuot racdaw y'r neuad; a guedy y dyuot y gynted y neuad kyuarch guell a wnaeth y Wawl uab Clut a'y gedymdeithon o wyr a gwraged.
sentences.l: And when he-knew their being at the beginning of carousing after eating, coming forward to the hall; and after his coming to the upper-end of the hall, greeting he-did to Gwawl son of-Clud and his companions of men and women.
sentences.i: And when he knew they were at the start of the drinking after the meal, he went on into the hall; and when he reached the upper end of the hall, he greeted Gwawl son of Clud and his companions, men and women.
sentences.n: pan wybu 'when he knew': gwybu, preterite of gwybot, softened after pan. y bot 'their being' = that they were; here y stands for eu 'their', which does not mutate (bot is unchanged). dyuot racdaw 'coming forward' — racdaw is rac conjugated, third person masculine, and the verbal noun carries the narrative with no finite verb. guedy y dyuot 'after his coming'. y Wawl 'to Gwawl', softened after y 'to'. o wyr a gwraged 'of men and women' (gwyr softened after o).

sentences.t: “Duw a ro da yt,” heb y Gwawl, “a chraessaw Duw wrthyt.”
sentences.l: “God may-he-give good to-you,” said Gwawl, “and welcome of-God to-you.”
sentences.i: “God give you good,” said Gwawl, “and God's welcome to you.”
sentences.n: Duw a ro 'may God give': ro is the present subjunctive of rodi, used for a wish. a chraessaw 'and welcome' — craessaw, another spelling of cressaw, with the spirant mutation after a. The greeting is the one Pwyll gave the stranger a year before.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ynteu, “Duw a dalo yt. Negessawl wyf wrthyt.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he-for-his-part, “God may-he-repay to-you. One-with-an-errand am-I to-you.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “may God repay you. I have an errand to you.”
sentences.n: heb ynteu 'said he for his part' marks the change of speaker. Duw a dalo yt 'may God repay you': talo is the present subjunctive of talu 'pay', softened after a. Negessawl 'having an errand' (neges + -awl), the predicate first.

sentences.t: “Craessaw wrth dy neges,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Welcome to your errand,” said he.
sentences.i: “Welcome to your errand,” he said.
sentences.n: Craessaw wrth dy neges 'welcome to your errand' — the greeting turned to the errand itself.

sentences.t: “Ac os arch gyuartal a erchy ymi, yn llawen ti a'e keffy.”
sentences.l: “And if a-request fair you-ask to-me, gladly you it-is-that will-get-it.”
sentences.i: “And if you ask a fair request of me, you shall have it gladly.”
sentences.n: Gwawl goes on speaking. os 'if'. arch gyuartal 'a fair request': kyuartal 'equal, fair, reasonable' softened after the feminine noun. a erchy 'that you ask' (second-person present). ti a'e keffy 'you will get it' — 'e is the infixed 'it', another spelling of 'y.

sentences.t: “Kyuartal, Arglwyd,” heb ynteu, “nyt archaf onyt rac eisseu. Sef arch a archaf, lloneit y got uechan a wely di o uwyt.”
sentences.l: “Fair, Lord,” said he-for-his-part, “I-do-not-ask except for want. That-is the request that I-ask: the-fill of the small bag that you-see of food.”
sentences.i: “A fair one, Lord,” he said. “I ask only out of need. The request I make is the bag's fill of food — the little bag you see.”
sentences.n: nyt archaf onyt rac eisseu 'I ask only for want': archaf, first-person present of erchi; onyt 'except'; eisseu 'want, lack'. Sef arch a archaf 'this is the request I ask' — Sef again. lloneit y got uechan 'the fill of the little bag', the words of Rhiannon's instruction. a wely di 'that you see': gwely, second-person present of gwelet, softened after the relative a. o uwyt 'of food'.

sentences.t: “Arch didraha yw honno,” heb ef, “a thi a'y keffy yn llawen. Dygwch uwyt idaw,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “A-request unarrogant is that,” said he, “and you it-is-that will-get-it gladly. Bring food to-him,” said he.
sentences.i: “That is a modest request,” he said, “and you shall have it gladly. Bring him food,” he said.
sentences.n: Arch didraha yw honno 'a modest request is that' — the predicate first, then yw. didraha 'without arrogance, modest' (di- + traha 'arrogance'). a thi 'and you', spirant after a. Dygwch is the plural imperative of dwyn 'bring'; uwyt is bwyt softened as the object.

sentences.t: Riuedi mawr o sswydwyr a gyuodassant y uynyd, a dechreu llenwi y got.
sentences.l: A-number great of officers it-was-that rose up, and beginning to-fill the bag.
sentences.i: A great number of officers rose up and began to fill the bag.
sentences.n: Riuedi 'number' (rhifedi). sswydwyr 'officers, servants of the court' — ss for s again (swyd 'office'). a gyuodassant 'rose' is kyuodassant, third-person plural preterite in -assant, softened after a; a fronted noun subject usually takes a singular verb (see Y meicheu a aeth below), but here the plural follows the sense of Riuedi mawr 'a great number'. y uynyd 'up' (mynyd 'mountain', 'to the mountain'). a dechreu 'and beginning' carries on in a verbal noun.

sentences.t: Ac yr a uyrit yndi ny bydei lawnach no chynt.
sentences.l: And for-all that was-thrown into-it, it-would-not-be fuller than before.
sentences.i: And however much was thrown in, it was no fuller than before.
sentences.n: yr a 'for all that, however much'. uyrit is byrit, the impersonal imperfect of bwrw 'throw' (-it), softened after a. ny bydei lawnach no chynt fulfils Rhiannon's promise in the same words.

sentences.t: “Eneit,” heb y Guawl, “a uyd llawn dy got ti uyth?”
sentences.l: “Soul,” said Gwawl, “will-be full your bag ever?”
sentences.i: “Friend,” said Gwawl, “will your bag ever be full?”
sentences.n: The question Rhiannon foretold, word for word: a uyd 'will … be?', with the question particle a softening byd. uyth 'ever' (byth softened, as adverbs often are).

sentences.t: “Na uyd, y rof a Duw,” heb ef, “yr a dotter yndi uyth, ony chyuyt dylyedauc tir a dayar a chyuoeth, a ssenghi a'y deudroet y bwyt yn y got a dywedut, ‘Digawn ry dodet yma.’”
sentences.l: “It-will-not-be, between me and God,” said he, “for-all that may-be-put into-it ever, unless rises a-nobleman of-land and earth and realm, and treading with his two-feet the food in the bag and saying, ‘Enough has-been-put here.’”
sentences.i: “No, between me and God,” he said, “not for all that may ever be put in it, unless a nobleman of land and territory and realm rises and treads the food down in the bag with both his feet and says, ‘Enough has been put in here.’”
sentences.n: y rof a Duw 'between me and God' — y rof is y rwng conjugated, first person; this oath recurs. yr a dotter 'for all that may be put': dotter is the impersonal present subjunctive of dodi (-er). dylyedauc tir a dayar a chyuoeth 'a nobleman of land and earth and realm' — Pwyll changes Rhiannon's tra chyuoethauc into a phrase Gwawl cannot refuse. ssenghi is sengi 'tread' again, spelt with ss and ngh.

sentences.t: “A geimat,” heb y Riannon, “kyuot y uynyd ar uyrr,” wrth Gwawl vab Clut.
sentences.l: “O champion(?),” said Rhiannon, “rise up quickly,” to Gwawl son of-Clud.
sentences.i: “Champion,” said Rhiannon to Gwawl son of Clud, “get up quickly.”
sentences.n: A geimat: A is the vocative particle 'O', which softens the noun after it, as in A wyr 'O men' (the last part): geimat is keimat softened. keimat is a word of disputed meaning: it is usually taken as 'champion, warrior' (compare later ceimiad), but some read it as a looser form of address; 'champion' is a guess from the setting. kyuot is the imperative of kyuodi; ar uyrr 'quickly' (byrr 'short', softened after ar). wrth Gwawl: wrth normally softens (wrth Wawl, as y Wawl elsewhere), but the name is left unmutated. vab is uab, the scribe here writing v for the sound u stands for elsewhere.

sentences.t: “Kyuodaf yn llawen,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “I-will-rise gladly,” said he.
sentences.i: “I will rise gladly,” he said.
sentences.n: Kyuodaf 'I will rise', the first-person present of kyuodi with future sense — the answer echoes the command.

sentences.t: A chyuodi y uynyd, a dodi y deudroet yn y got, a troi o Pwyll y got yny uyd Guawl dros y penn yn y got ac yn gyflym caeu y got, a llad clwm ar y carryeu, a dodi llef ar y gorn.
sentences.l: And rising up, and putting his two-feet in the bag, and turning by Pwyll the bag until is Gwawl over his head in the bag, and swiftly closing the bag, and tying a-knot on the thongs, and putting a-cry on his horn.
sentences.i: He rose and put both his feet in the bag, and Pwyll turned the bag until Gwawl was over his head in it, and swiftly shut the bag, tied a knot in the thongs, and sounded a blast on his horn.
sentences.n: A whole action told in verbal nouns, every step Rhiannon foretold. troi o Pwyll 'turning by Pwyll': the subject of a verbal noun is marked with o. a troi: the spirant mutation after a (a throi) is not written here. yny uyd 'until he is': byd, softened after yny, a present tense for the vivid moment. yn gyflym 'swiftly'. caeu 'shut'. llad clwm 'tie a knot', as in Rhiannon's instruction. y gorn 'his horn' (corn softened after y 'his').

sentences.t: Ac ar yny, llyma y teulu am penn y llys, ac yna kymryt pawb o'r niuer a doeth y gyt a Guawl, a'y dodi yn y carchar e hun.
sentences.l: And thereupon (as written: ar yny), behold the household-troop upon the court, and then taking each of the company that came together with Gwawl, and putting-them in his own prison.
sentences.i: And thereupon, there was the warband down upon the court; and then every one of the company who had come with Gwawl was taken and put in his own prison.
sentences.n: Ac ar yny: so the manuscript reads; it is a slip for Ac ar hynny 'and thereupon', the phrase the tale uses everywhere else (the Red Book has ar hynny here), and it is glossed as that. llyma 'behold, here is'. am penn y llys 'down upon the court', written here with penn. kymryt pawb o'r niuer 'taking all of the company' — the verbal noun with no stated subject. y gyt a 'together with'. a'y dodi 'and putting them'. yn y carchar e hun 'in his own prison': the reading is uncertain. e hun is 'himself, his own'; 'his' would soften carchar (y garchar, as the Red Book has), so the White Book's carchar either leaves the mutation unwritten or has the article, 'in the prison by himself'. Whose prison is not said: taken with pawb, it may be each man in a prison of his own; it may be the prison of the court. The l and i keep 'his own' and do not decide.

sentences.t: A bwrw y bratteu a'r loppaneu a'r yspeil didestyl y amdanaw a oruc Pwyll.
sentences.l: And throwing the rags and the clumsy-boots and the gear shabby(?) from-about-him Pwyll did.
sentences.i: And Pwyll threw off the rags and the clumsy boots and the shabby gear he had on.
sentences.n: bwrw … a oruc Pwyll 'throwing … Pwyll did' = he threw. loppaneu is the lloppaneu of the disguise, here written with a single l. yspeil 'gear, garments' (the same word as yspeil 'spoil'). didestyl is a rare word of uncertain meaning, probably 'shabby, unseemly'; it is taken here from the context of the disguise. y amdanaw 'from about him': y 'from' + amdanaw.

sentences.t: Ac mal y delei pob un o'e niuer ynteu y mywn, y trawei pob un dyrnawt ar y got, ac y gouynnei, “Beth yssyd ymma?”
sentences.l: And as would-come each one of his company for-his-part in, would-strike each one a-blow on the bag, and would-ask, “What is here?”
sentences.i: And as each man of Pwyll's company came in, he would strike a blow on the bag and ask, “What is in here?”
sentences.n: mal y delei 'as … would come': mal = ual 'as'; delei is the imperfect subjunctive of dyuot. o'e niuer ynteu 'of his own company' — Pwyll's men, with ynteu pointing back to him. y trawei 'would strike' and y gouynnei 'would ask' are imperfects of taraw and gouyn: the imperfect is the tense of things done again and again. dyrnawt 'blow'. Beth yssyd ymma? 'what is here?'

sentences.t: “Broch,” medynt wynteu.
sentences.l: “A-badger,” say they-for-their-part.
sentences.i: “A badger,” the others would say.
sentences.n: medynt 'they say' comes from the defective verb med- 'say', used only in a few forms. wynteu 'they for their part' — the men already inside answer the newcomer.

sentences.t: Sef kyfryw chware a wneynt, taraw a wnai pob un dyrnawt ar y got, ae a'e droet ae a throssawl; ac y uelly guare a'r got a wnaethont.
sentences.l: That-is the kind-of game that they-would-make: striking would-do each one a-blow on the bag, either with his foot or with a-cudgel; and thus playing with the bag they-did.
sentences.i: They played a game of this kind: each one would strike a blow on the bag, with his foot or with a cudgel; and so they played with the bag.
sentences.n: Sef kyfryw chware a wneynt 'this is the kind of game they would make' (wneynt, imperfect plural of gwneuthur). chware and guare are two spellings of the same word, 'game, play' (modern chwarae). taraw a wnai 'striking would do' — the verbal-noun pattern with the imperfect wnai. ae … ae 'either … or'. a'e droet 'with his foot' (troet softened after 'e 'his'). a throssawl 'with a cudgel' (trossawl, spirant after a 'with').

sentences.t: Pawb, ual y delei, a ouynnei, “Pa chware a wnewch chwi uelly?”
sentences.l: Everyone, as he-would-come, would-ask, “What game do-you-make thus?”
sentences.i: Everyone, as he came, would ask, “What game is this you are playing?”
sentences.n: a ouynnei 'would ask': gouynnei, imperfect, the g lost after a. Pa chware 'what game' — ch does not mutate after pa. a wnewch chwi 'that you make' (second-person plural present).

sentences.t: “Guare broch yg got,” medynt wynteu.
sentences.l: “Playing badger in-a bag,” say they-for-their-part.
sentences.i: “Badger in the bag,” they would say.
sentences.n: Guare broch yg got 'playing badger in bag'. yg got is yn 'in' + cot with nasal mutation (modern yng nghod): the scribe writes yg for yng, and g for the mutated ngh. The game's name is used as a fixed phrase.

sentences.t: Ac yna gyntaf y guarywyt broch yg got.
sentences.l: And then first was-played badger in-a bag.
sentences.i: And that was the first time Badger in the Bag was played.
sentences.n: gyntaf 'first' is kyntaf softened, as adverbs often are. y guarywyt 'was played' is the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of guare. The tale claims to tell the origin of a game called broch yg got; whether such a game was really played in medieval Wales is not known from any other source, and the explanation may be the storyteller's own.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb y gwr o'r got, “pei guarandawut uiui, nyt oed dihenyd arnaf uy llad y mywn got.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said the man from the bag, “if you-would-listen to-me, it-was-not a-fit-death on-me my killing in a bag.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” said the man in the bag, “if you would listen to me — it is no fit death for me, to be killed in a bag.”
sentences.n: y gwr o'r got 'the man from the bag' — Gwawl is not named while he is inside it. pei 'if' with guarandawut, the second-person imperfect subjunctive of guarandaw 'listen' (-ut). uiui 'me', the emphatic pronoun softened. dihenyd 'end, death', especially the death a man deserves. uy llad 'my killing' = to kill me, the possessive as object of the verbal noun.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb Euey Hen, “guir a dyweit. Iawn yw yt y warandaw; nyt dihenyt arnaw hyny.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said Hefeydd the-Old, “true he-says. Right is for-you to listen-to-him; it-is-not a-fit-death on-him, that.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” said Hefeydd the Old, “he speaks the truth. It is right for you to listen to him; that is no fit death for him.”
sentences.n: Euey Hen: so the manuscript reads, without the final d; it is a slip for Eueyd Hen, Hefeydd the Old (the Red Book has eveyd hen). guir a dyweit 'true (it is that) he says' — the object first; dyweit is the third-person present of dywedut. y warandaw 'to listen to him': gwarandaw softened after y 'his', the object as a possessive. dihenyt is dihenyd with the final d written t. hyny is the manuscript's spelling of hynny 'that', with one n (the Red Book has hynny); kept as written.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb y Pwyll, “mi a wnaf dy gynghor di amdanaw ef.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said Pwyll, “I it-is-that will-do your counsel about-him.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Pwyll, “I will follow your counsel about him.”
sentences.n: Ie 'yes'. mi a wnaf dy gynghor di 'I will do your counsel': kynghor softened after dy. amdanaw ef 'about him', am conjugated with the pronoun repeated.

sentences.t: “Llyna dy gynghor di,” heb Riannon yna.
sentences.l: “There-is your counsel,” said Rhiannon then.
sentences.i: “Here is the counsel for you,” said Rhiannon then.
sentences.n: Rhiannon steps in with the counsel herself. Llyna dy gynghor di 'there is your counsel' — that is, 'here is what I counsel you'. heb Riannon: the name without the article y this time. The speech continues in the next unit.

sentences.t: “Yd wyt yn y lle y perthyn arnat llonydu eircheit a cherdoryon. Gat yno ef y rodi drossot y pawb,” heb hi, “a chymer gedernit y ganthaw na bo ammouyn na dial uyth amdanaw, a digawn yw hynny o gosp arnaw.”
sentences.l: “You-are in the place where it-belongs on-you to-satisfy petitioners and minstrels. Leave there him to give on-your-behalf to everyone,” said she, “and take a-pledge from-him that there-be-not seeking nor vengeance ever about-it, and enough is that of punishment on-him.”
sentences.i: “You are in a place where it falls to you to satisfy petitioners and minstrels. Let him give to everyone there on your behalf,” she said, “and take a pledge from him that there shall never be any claim or vengeance for this; and that is punishment enough for him.”
sentences.n: Yd wyt 'you are', with yd before the vowel. y perthyn arnat 'where it belongs on you' = it is your duty. llonydu 'satisfy, content' (llonyd 'content'). eircheit is the plural of eirchat 'petitioner'; a cherdoryon 'and minstrels' (kerdoryon, spirant after a). Gat is the imperative of gadu 'let, leave'. drossot 'for you, on your behalf' is tros conjugated, second person. a chymer 'and take' (kymer, imperative). gedernit is kedernit 'surety, pledge', softened as object. y ganthaw 'from him'. na bo 'that there may not be'. ammouyn 'seeking (redress)'. o gosp 'of punishment' (cosp softened after o).

sentences.t: “Ef a geif hynny yn llawen,” heb y gwr o'r got.
sentences.l: “He it-is-that will-get that gladly,” said the man from the bag.
sentences.i: “He shall have that gladly,” said the man in the bag.
sentences.n: Ef a geif 'he will get': keif, the third-person present of caffael, softened after a. Gwawl speaks of Pwyll in the third person — 'he (your lord) shall have it'.

sentences.t: “A minheu a'e kymmeraf yn llawen,” heb y Pwyll, “gan gynghor Heueyd a Riannon.”
sentences.l: “And I-for-my-part it-is-that will-take-it gladly,” said Pwyll, “with the counsel of Hefeydd and Rhiannon.”
sentences.i: “And I will accept it gladly,” said Pwyll, “on the counsel of Hefeydd and Rhiannon.”
sentences.n: A minheu 'and I for my part'. a'e kymmeraf 'will take it': 'e the infixed 'it', kymmeraf the first-person present of kymryt. gan gynghor 'with the counsel of' — kynghor softened after gan.

sentences.t: “Kynghor yw hynny gynnym ni,” heb wynt.
sentences.l: “Counsel is that with-us,” said they.
sentences.i: “That is our counsel,” they said.
sentences.n: Kynghor yw hynny gynnym ni 'counsel is that with us' = that is our counsel — the predicate first. gynnym is gan conjugated, first person plural, with ni repeated. heb wynt 'said they'.

sentences.t: “Y gymryt a wnaf,” heb y Pwyll.
sentences.l: “Its taking I-will-do,” said Pwyll.
sentences.i: “I will accept it,” said Pwyll.
sentences.n: Y gymryt a wnaf 'its taking I will do' = I will take it: kymryt softened after y 'its', the object as a possessive, then a wnaf in place of a finite verb.

sentences.t: “Keis ueicheu drossot.”
sentences.l: “Seek sureties on-your-behalf.”
sentences.i: “Find sureties for yourself.”
sentences.n: Pwyll goes on, to Gwawl. Keis is the imperative of keissaw 'seek'. ueicheu is meicheu 'sureties', plural of mach, softened as the object. drossot 'for you'.

sentences.t: “Ni a uydwn drostaw,” heb Heueyd, “yny uo ryd y wyr y uynet drostaw.”
sentences.l: “We it-is-that will-be for-him,” said Hefeydd, “until may-be free his men to go for-him.”
sentences.i: “We will stand for him,” said Hefeydd, “until his own men are free to stand for him.”
sentences.n: Ni a uydwn 'we will be': bydwn, first-person plural future of bot, softened after a. drostaw 'over him, for him' is tros conjugated, third person masculine — standing surety 'for' a man. yny uo ryd 'until it be free' (bo, subjunctive). y wyr 'his men' (gwyr softened after y 'his') — they are in prison.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny y gollyngwyt ef o'r got ac y rydhawyt y oreugwyr.
sentences.l: And thereupon was-released he from the bag and were-freed his best-men.
sentences.i: And thereupon he was let out of the bag, and his chief men were set free.
sentences.n: Ac ar hynny 'and thereupon', the phrase written correctly this time. y gollyngwyt 'was released' and y rydhawyt 'were freed' are impersonal preterites in -wyt (gollwng, rydhau). y oreugwyr 'his best men' — goreugwyr (goreu 'best' + gwyr), its g lost after y 'his'.

sentences.t: “Gouyn ueithon y Wawl weicheu,” heb yr Heueyd.
sentences.l: “Ask now of Gwawl sureties,” said Hefeydd.
sentences.i: “Now ask Gwawl for sureties,” said Hefeydd.
sentences.n: Gouyn is the imperative of gouyn 'ask'. ueithon 'now, at this point'. y Wawl 'of Gwawl', softened after y. weicheu is meicheu again, softened as the object; the scribe writes w here where he wrote u in ueicheu above — the same v sound. heb yr Heueyd: the article as yr before h.

sentences.t: “Ni a adwaenwn y neb a dylyer y kymryt y ganthaw.”
sentences.l: “We it-is-that know the ones that ought to be-taken from-him.”
sentences.i: “We know which men ought to be taken from him.”
sentences.n: Hefeydd goes on speaking. Ni a adwaenwn 'we know' — adwaenwn is the first-person plural present of adnabod 'know (a person)'. y neb a dylyer y kymryt 'those whom it is right to take': dylyer is the impersonal present subjunctive of dylyu 'ought'. y kymryt 'their taking' = to take them: y is for eu 'their', so kymryt is unmutated.

sentences.t: Riuaw y meicheu a wnaeth Heueyd.
sentences.l: Counting the sureties did Hefeydd.
sentences.i: Hefeydd counted out the sureties.
sentences.n: Riuaw 'counting, enumerating' (rhifo) + a wnaeth 'did'. y meicheu 'the sureties': the article does not soften a plural noun.

sentences.t: “Llunnya dy hunn,” heb y Guawl, “dy ammot.”
sentences.l: “Shape yourself,” said Gwawl, “your terms.”
sentences.i: “Frame your terms yourself,” said Gwawl.
sentences.n: Llunnya is the imperative of llunyaw 'shape, frame'. dy hunn 'yourself'. ammot 'covenant, terms'. The tag splits the command from its object.

sentences.t: “Digawn yw gennyf i,” heb y Pwyll, “ual y llunnyawd Riannon.”
sentences.l: “Enough is with-me,” said Pwyll, “as Rhiannon framed.”
sentences.i: “It is enough for me,” said Pwyll, “as Rhiannon framed them.”
sentences.n: Digawn yw gennyf i 'enough it is with me' = I am content. ual y llunnyawd 'as she framed (it)': llunnyawd is the third-person preterite in -awd.

sentences.t: Y meicheu a aeth ar yr ammot hwnnw.
sentences.l: The sureties it-was-that went on that covenant.
sentences.i: The sureties went bond on those terms.
sentences.n: Y meicheu a aeth: in the abnormal sentence a plural noun subject usually takes a singular verb (aeth 'went', not aethant); a pronoun subject takes a plural one (wynt a welynt above), and a noun of plural sense sometimes does (Riuedi mawr … a gyuodassant). mynet ar 'go on' (a covenant) is to stand bound by it.

sentences.t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb y Guawl, “briwedic wyf i, a chymriw mawr a geueis, ac ennein yssyd reit ymi, ac y ymdeith yd af i, gan dy gannyat ti. A mi a adawaf wyrda drossof yma, y attep y pawb o'r a'th ouynno di.”
sentences.l: “Yes, Lord,” said Gwawl, “bruised am I, and a-hurt great I-got, and a-bath is need to-me, and away I-go, with your leave. And I it-is-that will-leave noblemen on-my-behalf here, to answer to everyone of those that may-ask-you.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Lord,” said Gwawl, “I am bruised, and I have taken great hurt, and I am in need of a bath, and I will go away, with your leave. And I will leave noblemen here in my place, to answer anyone who makes a claim on you.”
sentences.n: briwedic 'bruised, broken', a participle in -edic, put first. a chymriw mawr a geueis 'and great hurt I got': kymriw 'injury, crushing' with the spirant after a; keueis is the first-person preterite of caffael, softened. ennein 'bath, ointment'; yssyd reit ymi 'is a need to me'. y ymdeith 'away'. gan dy gannyat 'with your leave' (kannyat softened after dy). a adawaf 'will leave' (adaw). drossof 'on my behalf', tros conjugated, first person. o'r a'th ouynno 'of those who may ask you': 'th is the infixed 'you', gouynno the present subjunctive of gouyn, softened.

sentences.t: “Yn llawen,” heb y Pwyll, “a gwna ditheu hynny.”
sentences.l: “Gladly,” said Pwyll, “and do you-for-your-part that.”
sentences.i: “Gladly,” said Pwyll, “and do so.”
sentences.n: gwna 'do', the imperative, with ditheu (titheu softened after it) 'you for your part'.

sentences.t: Guawl a aeth parth a'y gyuoeth.
sentences.l: Gwawl it-was-that went towards his realm.
sentences.i: Gwawl went off towards his realm.
sentences.n: Guawl a aeth 'Gwawl went', the abnormal sentence. parth a'y gyuoeth 'towards his realm' (kyuoeth softened after 'y).

sentences.t: Y neuad ynteu a gyweirwyt y Pwyll a'e niuer, ac yniuer y llys y am hynny.
sentences.l: The hall for-its-part was-prepared for Pwyll and his company, and the company of the court around that.
sentences.i: The hall, for its part, was made ready for Pwyll and his company, and for the company of the court besides.
sentences.n: Y neuad … a gyweirwyt 'the hall … was prepared': the subject first and then an impersonal preterite in -wyt (kyweirwyt, softened after a). ynteu after the noun turns the story back to Pwyll's party. yniuer 'company' (niuer with prefixed y). y am hynny 'besides'.

sentences.t: Ac y'r bordeu yd aethont y eisted, ac ual yd eistedyssant ulwydyn o'r nos honno, yd eistedwys paub y nos.
sentences.l: And to the tables they-went to sit, and as they-sat a-year from that night, sat everyone the night.
sentences.i: And they went to the tables to sit, and as they had sat a year before that night, so each one sat that night.
sentences.n: yd aethont 'they went' (another spelling of aethant). ual yd eistedyssant … yd eistedwys 'as they sat … sat': eistedyssant is the plural preterite, eistedwys the singular with pawb 'everyone'. ulwydyn o'r nos honno 'a year from that night' (blwydyn softened, a time phrase). paub is pawb spelt with u. y nos 'the night': the manuscript has no honno 'that' here (the Red Book has y nos honno), and none is supplied — the sense does not need it.

sentences.t: Bwyta a chyuedach a wnaethont, ac amser a doeth y uynet y gyscu.
sentences.l: Eating and carousing they-did, and time it-was-that came to go to sleep.
sentences.i: They ate and drank, and the time came to go to bed.
sentences.n: Bwyta a chyuedach a wnaethont, the formula of the first feast. amser a doeth 'time came', abnormal order. y uynet y gyscu 'to go to sleep' (mynet softened after y, kyscu likewise).

sentences.t: Ac y'r ystauell yd aeth Pwyll a Riannon, a threulaw y nos honno drwy digriuwch a llonydwch.
sentences.l: And to the chamber went Pwyll and Rhiannon, and spending that night through amusement and contentment.
sentences.i: And Pwyll and Rhiannon went to the chamber and spent that night in pleasure and contentment.
sentences.n: y'r ystauell 'to the chamber' first, so the verb takes yd. aeth is singular with the two names after it: a verb placed before its subject is regularly singular. a threulaw 'and spending' (treulaw, spirant after a). drwy 'through' (trwy). digriuwch is digrifwch spelt with u; llonydwch 'contentment, peace'.

sentences.t: A thrannoeth, yn ieuengtit y dyd, “Arglwyd,” heb Riannon, “kyuot y uynyd, a dechreu lonydu y kerdoryon, ac na ommed neb hediw, o'r a uynno da.”
sentences.l: And next-day, in the youth of the day, “Lord,” said Rhiannon, “rise up, and begin to-satisfy the minstrels, and do-not-refuse anyone today, of those that may-wish goods.”
sentences.i: And the next day, in the young part of the day, “Lord,” said Rhiannon, “rise up and begin to satisfy the minstrels, and refuse no one today who wants a gift.”
sentences.n: A thrannoeth 'and the next day' (trannoeth, spirant after a); yn ieuengtit y dyd 'in the youth of the day', early morning, as in the first part. kyuot y uynyd 'rise up'. dechreu lonydu 'begin to satisfy' (llonydu softened as object of dechreu). na ommed 'do not refuse': the negative imperative of gommed, its g lost after na. hediw 'today'. o'r a uynno da 'of those who may want goods': uynno is mynno, present subjunctive of mynnu, softened.

sentences.t: “Hynny a wnaf i, yn llawen,” heb y Pwyll, “a hediw a pheunyd tra parhao y wled honn.”
sentences.l: “That I-will-do, gladly,” said Pwyll, “and today and every-day while lasts this feast.”
sentences.i: “That I will do gladly,” said Pwyll, “today and every day while this feast lasts.”
sentences.n: Hynny a wnaf i 'that I will do' — the object first. a pheunyd 'and every day' (peunyd, spirant after a). tra parhao 'while it may last': parhao is the present subjunctive of parhau.

sentences.t: Ef a gyuodes Pwyll y uynyd, a pheri dodi gostec, y erchi y holl eircheit a cherdoryon dangos, a menegi udunt y llonydit pawb o honunt wrth y uod a'y uympwy; a hynny a wnaethpwyd.
sentences.l: He it-was-that rose, Pwyll, up, and causing to-put a-call-for-silence, to ask all the petitioners and minstrels to-show-themselves, and telling to-them that would-be-satisfied each of-them according-to his will and his whim; and that was-done.
sentences.i: Pwyll rose and had silence called, bidding all the petitioners and minstrels come forward and telling them that every one of them would be satisfied according to his will and his fancy; and so it was done.
sentences.n: Ef a gyuodes Pwyll 'he rose, Pwyll' — the pronoun anticipates the name. gyuodes is kyuodes, preterite in -es, softened after a. a pheri dodi gostec 'and causing a proclamation to be made' (peri, spirant after a); gostec is a call for silence before an announcement. dangos 'show (themselves)'. udunt 'to them', y conjugated, third person plural. y llonydit 'that would be satisfied': llonydit is the impersonal imperfect (-it) of llonydu. wrth y uod a'y uympwy 'according to his will and his whim' (bod, mympwy softened after 'his'). a wnaethpwyd, the impersonal preterite, here written with final d.

sentences.t: Y wled honno a dreulwyt, ac ny ommedwyt neb tra barhaud.
sentences.l: That feast was-spent, and was-not-refused anyone while it-lasted.
sentences.i: That feast was spent, and no one was refused while it lasted.
sentences.n: a dreulwyt and ny ommedwyt are impersonal preterites (-wyt) of treulaw 'spend' and gommed 'refuse' (the g lost after ny). tra barhaud 'while it lasted': parhaud, preterite in -aud, written here with b, though tra parhao in the last unit was left unmutated.

sentences.t: A phan daruu y wled, “Arglwyd,” heb y Pwyll wrth Heueyd, “mi a gychwynnaf, gan dy gannyat, parth a Dyuet auore.”
sentences.l: And when ended the feast, “Lord,” said Pwyll to Hefeydd, “I it-is-that will-set-out, with your leave, towards Dyfed tomorrow.”
sentences.i: And when the feast was over, “Lord,” said Pwyll to Hefeydd, “I will set out for Dyfed tomorrow, with your leave.”
sentences.n: pan daruu 'when (it) ended': daruu is the preterite of daruot 'end, come to pass'. mi a gychwynnaf 'I will set out' (kychwynnaf softened after a). parth a Dyuet 'towards Dyfed'. auore 'tomorrow'.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb Heueyd, “Duw a rwydhao ragot; a gwna oet a chyfnot y del Riannon i'th ol.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said Hefeydd, “God may-he-speed before-you; and make a-time and a-term that Rhiannon may-come after-you.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Hefeydd, “God speed you; and appoint a time and a day for Rhiannon to follow you.”
sentences.n: Duw a rwydhao ragot 'may God make easy before you': rwydhao is rhwydhao, softened after a, the present subjunctive of rhwydhau 'make easy, speed' (rhwydd 'easy'), a wish; ragot is rac 'before' conjugated, second person. oet a chyfnot 'a tryst and a term' (kyfnot, spirant after a). y del 'that she may come' (del, present subjunctive of dyuot). i'th ol 'after you' (yn ol 'behind').

sentences.t: “Y rof i a Duw,” heb ynteu Pwyll, “y gyt y kerdwn odymma.”
sentences.l: “Between me and God,” said he-for-his-part Pwyll, “together we-will-go from-here.”
sentences.i: “Between me and God,” said Pwyll, “we will go from here together.”
sentences.n: Y rof i a Duw 'between me and God', the oath with the pronoun i this time. heb ynteu Pwyll 'said he for his part, Pwyll'. y gyt 'together'. y kerdwn 'we will go' (kerdet), first-person plural present with future sense. odymma 'from here'.

sentences.t: “Ay uelly y mynny di, Arglwyd?” heb yr Heueyd.
sentences.l: “Is-it thus that you-wish, Lord?” said Hefeydd.
sentences.i: “Is that how you wish it, Lord?” said Hefeydd.
sentences.n: Ay is the question particle a with y: 'is it …?'. uelly 'thus'. y mynny di 'that you wish' (mynny, second-person present of mynnu).

sentences.t: “Uelly, y rof a Duw,” heb y Pwyll.
sentences.l: “Thus, between me and God,” said Pwyll.
sentences.i: “Just so, between me and God,” said Pwyll.
sentences.n: Uelly 'thus' — Pwyll answers by taking up Hefeydd's own word, the Welsh way of saying yes, and seals it with the oath once more.

about: A year after their first meeting Pwyll comes with a hundred horsemen to the court of Hefeydd the Old to claim Rhiannon, and at the wedding feast rashly promises a stranger whatever he asks; the stranger is Gwawl son of Clud, her rejected suitor, and he asks for Rhiannon and the feast. Rhiannon puts Gwawl off for a year and gives Pwyll a little bag that no food can fill, and at Gwawl's own feast Pwyll, dressed as a beggar, tricks him into the bag while his men beat it in the first game of ‘badger in the bag’. Gwawl buys his release with sureties and a promise of no vengeance, Pwyll and Rhiannon keep their wedding night, and Pwyll makes ready to take her home to Dyfed.
